newsitem.title: CHINA: China sees UK election boost to Sino-British trade.
newsitem.headline: China sees UK election boost to Sino-British trade.

text.p: Britain's election of a Labour government could boost trade ties with China after 18 years of Conservative rule in which relations cooled, mainly amid disputes over Hong Kong, the China Daily said on Sunday.

The presence of newly elected British Prime Minister Tony Blair at ceremonies to mark Hong Kong's handover to Beijing at midnight on June 30 could nurture trade, the China Daily Business Weekly quoted senior trade researcher Song Jian as saying.

"The Labour government should seize the opportunity to distance its China policies from its predecessor and expand bilateral trade ties, which is in the interest of both countries," said Song, of the International Trade Research Institute under the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.
Blair's election win and China's resumption of sovereignty over Hong Kong on July 1 after 156 years of British colonial rule left Britain better placed to boost trade ties with China, said Song,

"If Blair is present at the grand ceremony on July 1 as he has hinted, it will consolidate the new government's reputation and be conducive to a successful transition of Hong Kong and two-way trade," Song was quoted as saying.

The government trade researcher hinted that Labour could benefit from the fact that any blame for difficulties in the handover process would be laid at the door of the losing Conservatives, who oversaw the handover negotiations.
"Hong Kong's return is a good opportunity for Labour because the party does not have to care about the previous thorny issues incurred by the Conservatives," Song said.
Song blamed the Conservatives for "contradictory" policies that had hampered trade.
"Although some progress was seen in the past year or two, trade volume between the two nations cannot be satisfying in regard to the economic power of both sides," Song said.
Bilateral trade rose 6.5 percent to $5.1 billion last year, ranking Britain third among China's European Union trading partners, the newspaper said. It gave no more details.
Song warned Britain not to ignore the fact that it had fallen behind some of its European competitors, notably Germany, in trading with China.

His remarks came as French President Jacques Chirac leaves China at the end of a four-day state visit that witnessed pledges on a joint global partnership into the 21st century and the signing of more than $1.8 billion in business deals for French and European businesses.
Ties between Britain and China soured in the early 1990s when Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten introduced democratic reforms in the territory without consulting Beijing.
China set up a provisional legislature in December that will replace the currently elected Legislative Council after the colony reverts to Beijing.
